doc.title: Lexical
doc.paragraph: The Lexical analyzer for Adaptive Framework is responsible for tokenizing Adaptive Scripts, Templates and Expressions as inputs for the parser. In this section, we will cover comments and whitespace, identifiers, keywords, operators, and literals.
The following are examples of both types of comments:
Whitespace are character sequences that are ignored by the lexical analyzer and serve the purpose of making code more readable. The following is a list of whitespace characters:

list.item: TAB character
Vertical Tab
Line Feed
Form Feed
Carriage Return
Zero Width No-Break Space
Space Separator
(Comments)

doc.paragraph: Identifiers are sequences of characters that are used to identify a variable name, category, function name, method name, parameter name, qualifier name symbol reference, interface name, type variable name, or object property name.
Identifiers have no length limit and are case-sensitive.
doc.code: Identifier ::= IdentifierStart IdentifierContinue* IdentifierStart ::= ID_START | '$' | '_' IdentifierContinue ::= ID_CONTINUE | '$' | ZWNJ | ZWJ

list.item: ID_START is any codepoint with ID_START flag
ID_CONTINUE is any codepoint with ID_CONTINUE flag
ZWNJ is the Zero-width Non-Joiner (0x200c)
ZWJ is the Zero-width Joiner (0x200d)

doc.paragraph: A name that starts with #, such as #compile, #pi, or #block, is a different kind of token, a pound identifier, and it cannot be used as a variable name. You write some of them yourself, like the #compile pragma and compiler literals such as #pi (see Language Features). Others, such as #block, are what you may see in decompile output, and are not something you write in normal scripts.
When declaring a variable name, you may use any identifier with the exception of the following reserved names:
doc.code: false INF Infinity NaN null true undefined break case catch const continue default do else extends finally for function if interface let return switch throw try type void while as async await class delete export from import in instanceof super this typeof var with
doc.paragraph: Literals are constants that can be used as values inside expressions. There are three types of literals:

list.item: Array Literal
Object Literal
Scalar Literal

doc.paragraph: An Array Literal is a sequence of literals, separated by , and enclosed in [ and ].
An Object Literal is a sequence of Identifier : Literal pairs, separated by , and enclosed by { and }.

A Scalar Literal may be a Double, an Integer, a String, true, false, null, or undefined. A regular expression literal (/a+b/i) is also a scalar literal; see Regular Expressions below. So is a typed literal, a string followed right away by a data type id, which is how you write a value of a data type that has no literal of its own, such as a date. Compiler literals such as #pi and #integerMax are described in Language Features.
Data Types and Conversion lists how to write a value of every data type, with the short forms such as dt.

An integer literal is a 64-bit integer, so it can be as large as 9223372036854775807; a larger one is a syntax error rather than a double. A number with a decimal point or an exponent, such as 1.5 or 1e3, is a double.
A literal is a value like any other, so you can use it right away: [1, 2][0] is 1, "abc"[1] is "b", and {a: 1}.a is 1.

A string literal is written between double quotes or single quotes; both mean the same thing. A template string, between backticks, can also hold substitutions (see Templates and Expressions). Inside any of them, a backslash starts an escape:

row.column: the code point with these two hex digits, here U+00E9 (é)
the code point with these four hex digits
the code point with this hex value, up to 10FFFF
nothing: the string continues on the next line

doc.paragraph: A backslash before any other character is that character, so "\q" is "q". A backslash and a digit from 1 to 9 is an error. A pair of \u escapes that spell a surrogate pair, such as "😀", is the one code point they stand for (😀); half of a pair on its own is an error, since a string holds code points.

Adaptive Script regular expressions are . Like everything else in AFW, they work on Unicode text: a pattern matches code points, not UTF-16 code units, so an emoji or any character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane is one character and never half of one. Classes such as \w, \d, and \b, and case-insensitive matching, follow Unicode for every language, and matching reads AFW's UTF-8 strings in place, with no conversion of the whole string. The syntax follows the Perl tradition that Python and Java also come from. Where ICU's Unicode rules give a different answer than XML Schema regular expressions, the notes at the end of this section say what to write; for ECMAScript's, see .

section.title: Writing a Pattern
section.paragraph: A regular expression literal is written /pattern/flags, where a value can start. Its value has data type regexp and is compiled once, when the script is compiled, so a pattern that does not compile is a syntax error at the literal, and using it costs no compile at run time. The pattern is passed to ICU as written: backslashes are not doubled. Write a / in the pattern as \/ or inside a class ([/]). After a value, / divides, and /= always divides and assigns.
The typed literal "a+b"re (or "a+b"regexp) is the same value, written as a string, so its backslashes are doubled: "\\d+"re is /\d+/.
A pattern matches anywhere in the value unless ^ and $ anchor it: test(/a+b/, "xaab") is true and test(/^a+b$/, "xaab") is false.

section.title: Flags

list.item: i ignores case, using Unicode case folding.
m lets ^ and $ match at the start and end of each line.
s lets . match a line terminator.
x ignores whitespace and # comments in the pattern.
u is accepted and changes nothing: patterns are always Unicode.

section.paragraph: Flags become part of the pattern: /a+b/i is "(?i)a+b"re. There is no g flag; replace takes a limit instead, and match_all finds every match.

section.title: Functions

list.item: test(regexp, value) is true if the regexp matches anywhere in value. value can be any text: a string, anyURI, dnsName, ipAddress, rfc822Name, or x500Name.
search(value, regexp) is the code point index of the first match, or -1, counted as index_of counts.
match(value, regexp) is the first match, or undefined.
match_all(value, regexp, limit?) is an array of every match, left to right; length(match_all(s, re)) counts them.
split(value, separator, limit?) and replace(value, search, replacement, limit?) take a string, which is literal text, or a regexp, which is a pattern.
regexp_escape(s) is s with every character that could have a meaning in a pattern escaped, to put data in a pattern.

section.paragraph: A match from match or match_all is an _AdaptiveRegexpMatch_ object: match is the matched text, index its code point index, captures[n] the text of group n (captures[0] is the whole match; a group that did not take part is undefined), and groups the text of each named group that took part (absent when the pattern has no named groups).

With a regexp, replace replaces the first match (limit 1 by default, -1 for every match). In the replacement, $1 is the text of group 1, $0 the whole match, ${name} a named group, and a backslash makes the next character literal (\$). With a string search the replacement is literal text too. The replacement can also be a function: it is called with each match's _AdaptiveRegexpMatch_ object and returns the string to put in. split with a regexp puts the text of each group after the piece before the match.

To use a pattern you have as a string, convert it once with to_regexp(s) and keep the result. A regexp value read from data is compiled each time a function uses it, unless you compile it once with compile<regexp>(r). A regexp is not called like a function: re(s) is an error, 're' is not a function; it is data type 'regexp'.
section.code: const date = /(?<y>\d{4})-(?<m>\d\d)-(?<d>\d\d)/; /^adm/->test("admin"); // true "on 2024-10-13"->search(date); // 3 "on 2024-10-13"->match(date).groups.m; // "10" length(match_all("a1b22c333", /\d+/)); // 3 "a, b ,c"->split(/\s*,\s*/); // ["a", "b", "c"] replace("2024-10-13", date, "${d}/${m}/${y}"); // "13/10/2024" replace("a1b22c333", /\d+/, "#", -1); // "a#b#c#" replace("2024-10-13", date, function (m) { return m.groups.d + "." + m.groups.m; }); // "13.10" to_regexp("^" + regexp_escape(name) + "\\z"); // name, literally

section.title: Match Limit
section.paragraph: ICU finds a match by backtracking, so some patterns, such as /^(a+)+$/ on a long run of a that does not end the way the pattern expects, take time that grows exponentially with the length of the value. A match stops after a fixed number of steps of the ICU match engine with a payload_too_large error, so a pattern, even one that arrives in a request, cannot hold a thread. The number is the process limit limitRegexpMatchSteps: 1000 by default, about a tenth of a second of backtracking, and far more than a linear scan of a long value needs. An application conf can change it like the other limit* settings (0 is unlimited), and process::limitRegexpMatchSteps shows the current value.

Because of an ICU issue, a lazy loop over a group that can match nothing, such as (b|)*? or (a?)+?, can reach the limit even on a short value (other regular expression engines answer it at once). Write the loop so its body cannot match empty: b*? instead of (b|)*?. ICU tracks this as , planned to be fixed in ICU 79.1; the cause is . For this case the limit is a workaround; for patterns that backtrack exponentially it is needed in any case.

Backtracking also needs memory, which ICU allocates itself. A match may use at most 8 MB for it, and at most half of what the request still has under limitRequestPoolBytes; one that needs more, such as /^(a|b)*$/ on a value of a few hundred thousand characters, stops with a payload_too_large error.

section.title: Coming from XML Schema Regular Expressions and fn:matches
section.paragraph: Earlier versions of AFW used XML Schema regular expressions. XPath fn:matches uses the same syntax with ^, $, and flags added.

list.item: A pattern matches anywhere in the value, as with fn:matches. An XML Schema pattern always had to match the whole value: write ^...\z for that.
Without the m flag, $ also matches just before a line terminator at the end of the value; fn:matches matches only at the end. Write \z for the very end.

\w is letters, marks, digits, and connector punctuation (in XML Schema, every character except punctuation, separators, and other), and \s is all Unicode white space (in XML Schema, space, tab, LF, and CR only).
The m flag and . use all the ICU line terminators, not only LF and CR, and the i flag uses full case folding.
The XML name escapes \i and \c are not ICU syntax, and class subtraction is written [a-z--[aeiou]] instead of [a-z-[aeiou]].
ICU also accepts lookahead, lookbehind, named groups, \b, and lazy and possessive quantifiers.
